short_definition: Rebalancing is the process of buying or selling investments to bring a portfolio back to its chosen target mix, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds, after market moves push it off course.
explanation: Rebalancing is needed because assets that grow faster take up a bigger share of a portfolio over time. There are two common ways to decide when to rebalance. One is a calendar schedule, such as once a year. The other is a drift band, where you act when an asset moves more than a set amount from its target, for example 5 percentage points. You can sell what has grown and buy what has lagged, or you can simply direct new contributions to the underweight asset.

Rebalancing matters because your asset allocation is a major driver of how much your portfolio can swing. If you never rebalance, a portfolio that started balanced can quietly become much riskier than you intended after a long run-up in stocks.

The main trade-offs of rebalancing are costs and taxes. Selling in a taxable account may trigger capital gains tax, and every trade can add fees and spreads. Rebalancing too often can cost more than it helps. It also doesn't guarantee higher returns, because its main job is controlling risk. Tax rules differ by country and account type, so check them before selling.
example: Illustrative example: you start with $10,000 split 60/40, which is $6,000 in stocks and $4,000 in bonds. A year later the stocks have grown to $7,500 and the bonds are still $4,000. The total is now $11,500, and stocks make up about 65%. Getting back to 60/40 means $6,900 in stocks and $4,600 in bonds. You could sell $600 of stocks and buy $600 of bonds, or add new money to bonds until the mix is back on target.
common_mistake: Making one of two opposite errors. The first is never rebalancing because the winning asset 'keeps going up', which lets risk creep up unnoticed. The second is rebalancing every few weeks, which piles up fees and possible taxes for little benefit.
title: Rebalancing
